extracted.intended_audience: USPTO patent examiners and patent practitioners (applicants and patent attorneys/agents)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for evaluating and supporting (or rebutting) obviousness rejections under 35 U.S.C. 103, including treatment of prior art, analogous art, applicant replies, and rebuttal evidence. Intended to direct examiner fact-finding, rationale articulation, and consideration of applicant submissions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Clear articulation of reasons for obviousness rejection
rubrics_metrics.description: The key to supporting any rejection under 35 U.S.C. 103 is the clear articulation of the reason(s) why the claimed invention would have been obvious.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rejections on obviousness cannot be sustained by mere conclusory statements; there must be articulated reasoning with some rational underpinning (KSR citing In re Kahn). Office personnel must make explicit the analysis supporting a 35 U.S.C. 103 rejection and articulate findings of fact that support the rationale relied upon.

rubrics_metrics.name: Combining prior art elements to yield predictable results
rubrics_metrics.description: Combining prior art elements according to known methods to yield predictable results may support a conclusion of obviousness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: See MPEP §2143 for examples illustrating how combining elements can support obviousness. Examiner should explain why combining references would have been obvious and whether results are predictable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Simple substitution of one known element for another
rubrics_metrics.description: Simple substitution of one known element for another to obtain predictable results may support obviousness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explain why the substitution is within ordinary skill and why predictable results would follow; cite supporting references or common knowledge where appropriate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of known technique to improve similar devices/methods/products
rubrics_metrics.description: Use of a known technique to improve similar devices (methods, or products) in the same way may support obviousness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Demonstrate that the technique is known in the relevant art and would have been applied in a predictable manner to the claimed device/product/method.

rubrics_metrics.name: Applying a known technique to a known device ready for improvement
rubrics_metrics.description: Applying a known technique to a known device (method, or product) ready for improvement to yield predictable results may support obviousness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Show why the device was 'ready for improvement' and that applying the known technique would predictably achieve the claimed result.

rubrics_metrics.name: 'Obvious to try' — finite predictable solutions with reasonable expectation of success
rubrics_metrics.description: 'Obvious to try' — choosing from a finite number of identified, predictable solutions, with a reasonable expectation of success may support obviousness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Applicable when the number of possible options is finite and predictable and there is a reasonable expectation one would succeed; explain predictability and expectation of success rather than mere possibility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Known work in one field prompting predictable variations in other fields
rubrics_metrics.description: Known work in one field of endeavor may prompt variations of it for use in either the same field or a different one based on design incentives or other market forces if the variations are predictable to one of ordinary skill in the art.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider cross-field design incentives/market forces and whether a person of ordinary skill would predictably vary the known work for the claimed use (KSR guidance).

rubrics_metrics.name: Teaching, suggestion, or motivation (TSM) supporting combination/modification
rubrics_metrics.description: Some teaching, suggestion, or motivation in the prior art that would have led one of ordinary skill to modify the prior art reference or to combine prior art reference teachings to arrive at the claimed invention may support obviousness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Although KSR cautioned against rigid TSM application, TSM remains a valid rationale. If TSM suffices, the examiner should use it; otherwise consider other rationales. Provide articulated factual basis for any asserted motivation to combine or modify.

rubrics_metrics.name: Applicant reply must distinctly and specifically point out errors
rubrics_metrics.description: 37 CFR 1.111(b) requires applicant to distinctly and specifically point out the supposed errors in the Office’s action and reply to every ground of objection and rejection in the Office action.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The reply must present arguments pointing out the specific distinction believed to render the claims patentable. A mere statement that a prima facie case was not established or unsupported assertions about common knowledge are not substantively adequate; traverse must include reasoned statement explaining why the examiner erred.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consider all timely rebuttal evidence when reevaluating obviousness
rubrics_metrics.description: Office personnel should consider all rebuttal evidence that is timely presented by the applicants when reevaluating any obviousness determination.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rebuttal evidence may include secondary considerations and unexpected results. After applicant's evidence is submitted, examiners must reconsider the obviousness determination in view of the entire record and review all rejections and proposed rejections for continued viability (see In re Piasecki, In re Eli Lilly). Follow procedures in MPEP §706.07(a) when deciding finality.

rubrics_metrics.name: Secondary considerations as evidence of nonobviousness
rubrics_metrics.description: Rebuttal evidence may include evidence of 'secondary considerations,' such as 'commercial success, long felt but unsolved needs, [and] failure of others', and may include evidence of unexpected results.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider weight of secondary considerations in context of other factual findings; examine whether such evidence rebuts the examiner's factual findings supporting obviousness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rebuttal evidence examples to show nonobviousness for combinations
rubrics_metrics.description: Applicants may submit evidence or argument to demonstrate that: (A) one of ordinary skill in the art could not have combined the claimed elements by known methods (e.g., due to technological difficulties); (B) the elements in combination do not merely perform the function that each element performs separately; or (C) the results of the claimed combination were unexpected.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If such evidence is presented, examiners should reconsider initial obviousness conclusions in view of the entire record and articulate how findings support continued rejections or why they do not.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prior art available under 35 U.S.C. 102 is available under 35 U.S.C. 103
rubrics_metrics.description: Subject matter that is prior art under 35 U.S.C. 102 can be used to support a rejection under section 103.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Admitted prior art can be relied upon for both anticipation and obviousness determinations regardless of statutory category. An obviousness rejection is based on applicable subsection(s) of 102 depending on the reference type and dates; applicants may overcome certain references (e.g., publications) by affidavits/declarations under 37 CFR 1.131. See MPEP §§901-901.06(d), §§2121-2129 for details.

rubrics_metrics.name: Content of prior art determined at time invention was made (avoid hindsight)
rubrics_metrics.description: The content of the prior art is determined 'at the time the invention was made' to avoid impermissible hindsight.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Decisionmaker should 'cast the mind back' to the relevant time and avoid hindsight bias. See MPEP §2145 for discussion of rebutting applicants' hindsight arguments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Evidence required to show 35 U.S.C. 103(c) applies (common ownership/joint research)
rubrics_metrics.description: An applicant seeking benefits of 35 U.S.C. 103(c) must establish that subject matter which only qualifies as prior art under subsection (e), (f) or (g) and the claimed invention were, at the time the invention was made, owned by the same person or subject to an obligation of assignment to the same person.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For joint research agreement benefits (applications pending on or after Dec. 10, 2004), applicant must show: (A) invention made by/on behalf of parties to an agreement effective on or before invention date; (B) invention made as result of activities within scope of the agreement; and (C) patent application discloses or is amended to disclose the parties' names. See MPEP §706.02(l)(2) and related case law (Ex parte Yoshino, In re Bartfeld).

rubrics_metrics.name: Reference must be analogous art to be relied on under 35 U.S.C. 103
rubrics_metrics.description: In order for a reference to be proper for use in an obviousness rejection under 35 U.S.C. 103, the reference must be analogous prior art to the claimed invention.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A reference is analogous art if (1) it is from the same field of endeavor as the claimed invention (even if addressing a different problem); or (2) it is reasonably pertinent to the problem faced by the inventor. 'Reasonably pertinent' means the reference would have logically commended itself to an inventor's attention in considering his problem. Examiners should consider the problem as reflected in the specification and may include a statement of the examiner's understanding of the problem to support analogy determinations (Bigio, Icon Health, In re Klein).

rubrics_metrics.name: Consider the problem framed by the specification when determining analogous art
rubrics_metrics.description: In determining whether a reference is reasonably pertinent, an examiner should consider the problem faced by the inventor as reflected—either explicitly or implicitly—in the specification.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the problem is viewed too narrowly or inconsistently with the specification, the scope of available prior art may be inappropriately limited. Examiner may need to explain why an inventor seeking to solve the identified problem would have looked to the reference.

rubrics_metrics.name: Weight similarities and differences in structure and function for analogy
rubrics_metrics.description: While classifications are some evidence, similarities and differences in structure and function of the inventions carry far greater weight in determining analogy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examiners should emphasize structural and functional overlap between references and claimed inventions when assessing whether references are analogous art (In re Ellis).

rubrics_metrics.name: Analogous art considerations across technical disciplines (chemical, mechanical, electrical, design)
rubrics_metrics.description: Examples across chemical, mechanical, electrical, and design arts illustrate how analogy is applied where problems and solutions overlap across related fields.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use discipline-specific precedents (e.g., Ex parte Bland, Stratoflex, Medtronic, In re Rosen) to inform whether references from other subfields are analogous based on the problem and solution commonality.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consider the claimed invention as a whole when assessing differences
rubrics_metrics.description: In determining the differences between the prior art and the claims, the question under 35 U.S.C. 103 is not whether the differences themselves would have been obvious, but whether the claimed invention as a whole would have been obvious.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Interpret claim language and consider both the invention and prior art references as a whole (see MPEP §§2111-2116.01 and relevant case law such as Stratoflex and In re Hirao). Avoid focusing solely on an isolated difference if other claim limitations or admitted unobvious steps exist.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not distill the invention to a 'gist' or 'thrust' (anti-pattern)
rubrics_metrics.description: Distilling the invention down to the 'gist' or 'thrust' of an invention disregards the 'as a whole' requirement and is improper.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid restricting consideration to a narrow conceptualization that excludes express claim limitations; ensure all claim limitations are considered rather than treating the claim as if it read differently (see W.L. Gore, Bausch & Lomb examples).
